nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the philosophical lyric and the poetry of the imagination
literary_identity: Poet; the great American philosophical poet of the century, an insurance executive who wrote the most sumptuous and abstract verse of the period.
biography: Born Wallace Stevens in Reading, Pennsylvania, on 2 October 1879; he studied at Harvard for three years and then at New York Law School, worked as a journalist and a lawyer, and joined the Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company in 1916, where he became vice-president in 1934 and remained until his death. Harmonium appeared in 1923, Ideas of Order in 1935, The Auroras of Autumn in 1950, and The Collected Poems in 1954; he won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award in 1955 and died in Hartford on 2 August 1955.
literary_profile: Stevens is the great American poet of the imagination: his poems ask, in the most sensuous language, what it means to make a world with the mind when the gods have gone. 'Sunday Morning', 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream', 'Anecdote of the Jar', 'The Idea of Order at Key West' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' are the central texts of American philosophical poetry, and his late long poems are among the most ambitious in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: The exotic and sumptuous vocabulary; the abstract argument carried by sensuous image; the blank verse paragraph and the unrhymed tercet; the single-colour image (blue, green, white) held until it becomes an idea; the aphorism and the late long poem.
intellectual_concerns: The imagination and reality; the death of God and the poetry that replaces religion; order, art and the made thing; the American landscape and the Florida sun; the body, desire and the weather; the ordinary and the supreme fiction.
historical_significance: Stevens is the central American philosophical poet of the century: Harmonium gave American poetry its most gorgeous surface, 'Sunday Morning' and 'Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction' established the imagination as the period's great subject, and his Collected Poems won every honour the country has. He is the period's most influential American poet after Eliot.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the objectivist lyric, the American idiom and the long poem of place
literary_identity: Poet and physician; the inventor of the American objectivist line and the author of Paterson, the great American long poem of place.
biography: Born William Carlos Williams in Rutherford, New Jersey, on 17 September 1883 of an English father and a Puerto Rican mother; he studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, where he met Pound and H. D., took his degree in 1906, and practised as a pediatrician in Rutherford for forty years while writing. He published Poems (1909), Al Que Quiere! (1917), Spring and All (1923), The Red Wheelbarrow (1923), An Early Martyr (1935), the first book of Paterson in 1946, and Pictures from Brueghel (1962), which won the Pulitzer Prize. He died in Rutherford on 4 March 1963.
literary_profile: Williams is the great American poet of the thing itself and of the spoken American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' is the period's most influential poetic programme. His short poems — 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'This Is Just to Say', 'Danse Russe' — are among the most imitated in the language, Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period, and Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land.
stylistic_characteristics: The line measured by the breath and broken by speech; the plain American word; the image without metaphor; the variable foot and the triadic stanza; the poem as a field of perception; the prose-and-verse collage of Spring and All and Paterson.
intellectual_concerns: The American place and the American idiom; the object and the thing seen without metaphor; the local city (Paterson, Rutherford); the body and desire; the immigrant and the working town; the poet as doctor and witness.
historical_significance: Williams is the founder of the American objectivist tradition and the great poet of the American idiom: 'no ideas but in things' changed American poetry, his short poems are the most imitated of the century, Spring and All is a foundational modernist text, and Paterson is the period's great American long poem. He is the poet through whom American poetry escaped the English line.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the syllabic poem, the accurate eye and the modernist menagerie
literary_identity: Poet, critic and editor; the great American poet of exact observation, the editor of The Dial, and the inventor of the syllabic stanza.
biography: Born Marianne Craig Moore in Kirkwood, Missouri, on 15 November 1887 and raised in Carlisle, Pennsylvania; she studied biology at Bryn Mawr, taught stenography and worked in a library before editing The Dial from 1925 to 1929. Poems (1921) was published by H.D. and Bryher without her knowledge; Observations followed in 1924, Selected Poems (with an introduction by Eliot) in 1935, and the Collected Poems in 1951, which won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award and the Bollingen Prize. She died in New York on 5 February 1972.
literary_profile: Moore is the great American poet of exact observation and of the moral weight of the precise word: her syllabic stanzas, her quotations embedded in her own text, her animals and baseball and armadillos, made a poetry of fact that is also a poetry of judgement. 'Poetry', 'The Fish', 'A Grave' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts, and her editorship of The Dial made her the period's most influential American editor.
stylistic_characteristics: The syllabic stanza counted by syllables and not by stress; the rhyme that falls inside the line; the quotation folded into the syntax; the exact zoological and botanical naming; the indented line and the elaborate stanza shape; the prose sentence broken into verse.
intellectual_concerns: Exact observation and the moral weight of fact; animals and the natural world; America, baseball and the ordinary hero; the sea and the shore; the poet's duty to be 'literal for the purposes of being allegorical'; modesty and self-deprecation.
historical_significance: Moore is one of the central American modernists: her syllabic stanza gave American poetry a new measure, her exact and quoted verse made fact a poetic value, and her fifteen years at The Dial made her the period's most important American editor. 'Poetry', 'The Fish' and 'The Pangolin' are permanent texts.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the modernist epic lyric and the poetry of the American sublime
literary_identity: Poet; the author of The Bridge, the most ambitious American long poem of the period and the great lyric poet of the American sublime.
biography: Born Harold Hart Crane at Garrettsville, Ohio, on 21 July 1899, the son of a candy manufacturer; he left school without a diploma, worked in advertising in Cleveland and New York, and published White Buildings in 1926. The Bridge appeared in 1930 to mixed reviews; he spent a year in Mexico on a Guggenheim fellowship and drowned himself from the steamship Orizaba in the Caribbean on 27 April 1932, aged thirty-two.
literary_profile: Crane wrote the most ambitious American long poem of the period and the greatest American lyric of the sublime: The Bridge attempted to answer The Waste Land with an American epic of the machine, the past and the imagination, and 'Voyages' and 'At Melville's Tomb' are among the finest shorter poems in modern American literature. His dense, prophetic style and his tragic death made him the emblem of the American poet destroyed by his own vision.
stylistic_characteristics: The dense, prophetic, syntactically compressed lyric; the extended metaphor held across a whole poem; the imagery of the sea, the bridge and the machine; the metrical experiment inside traditional stanza; the rhetoric of the American sublime.
intellectual_concerns: America and the American myth; the machine and the modern city; the sea and the voyage; memory, love and the loss of the beloved; the poet's vision and its cost; Whitman's inheritance and Eliot's counter-example.
historical_significance: Crane wrote the great American long poem of the period after Paterson and the finest American lyric of the sublime: The Bridge answered The Waste Land with an American epic, 'Voyages' is one of the great love poems in American literature, and his death at thirty-two made him the period's emblem of the poet destroyed by his vision.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the typographic lyric and the satire of the modern state
literary_identity: Poet and painter; the great experimenter of American typography, whose lower-case, punctuation-scattered lyrics made the printed page part of the poem.
biography: Born Edward Estlin Cummings in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 14 October 1894, the son of a Harvard professor and minister; he took his degrees at Harvard, served in the First World War as an ambulance driver, was interned by the French in 1917 for three months — the subject of The Enormous Room (1922) — and published Tulips and Chimneys (1923), & (1925), XLI Poems (1925) and Is 5 (1926). He painted, travelled in the Soviet Union (Eimi, 1933), won the Bollingen Prize in 1958 and the National Book Award in 1960, and died in North Conway, New Hampshire, on 3 September 1962.
literary_profile: Cummings is the period's great typographic poet: he made the page itself a unit of composition — the word broken across the line, the parenthesis, the lowercase 'i', the space that carries the pause — and his love lyrics ('somewhere i have never travelled,gladly beyond', 'i carry your heart with me') are among the most popular American poems of the century. His satire of the state ('next to of course god america i', 'i sing of Olaf glad and big') is the sharpest political verse of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The typographic page as a compositional unit; the word broken and the parenthesis; the lowercase pronoun and the deliberate misspelling; the sonnet and the ballad re-shaped by spacing; the syntax that must be read aloud to be understood; the satire delivered in the voice of its victim.
intellectual_concerns: Love and the private erotic world; the individual against the state and the army; satire of patriotism and bureaucracy; spring, roses, the moon and the natural world; the city and the crowd; death and the fragility of the person.
historical_significance: Cummings is the most popular experimental poet in English of the century: he made typography a poetic instrument, wrote the most-quoted American love lyrics after Frost, and produced the sharpest anti-war satire of the period. His work changed how poems are printed.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war lyric of the Jewish East End and the poetry of the painted image
literary_identity: Poet and painter; the greatest of the soldier-poets after Owen, the first major English poet of the Jewish immigrant poor.
biography: Born Isaac Rosenberg in Bristol on 25 November 1890, the son of Lithuanian Jewish immigrants, and brought up in the East End of London; he left school at fourteen to be an apprentice engraver, studied art at the Slade (1911–14) with Mark Gertler and David Bomberg, and published Night and Day (1912) and Youth (1915) at his own expense. He enlisted in 1915, served with the King's Own Royal Lancasters, and was killed at Fampoux on the Arras front on 1 April 1918; his Poems were collected in 1922.
literary_profile: Rosenberg is, with Owen, the greatest poet of the First World War and the first English poet to write out of the Jewish immigrant experience. 'Break of Day in the Trenches', 'Dead Man's Dump' and 'Returning, We Hear the Larks' are among the finest war poems in the language, and 'The Burning of the Temple' and the plays show a visionary ambition cut off at twenty-seven. He wrote from the ranks, not the officers' mess, and his poetry keeps the physical pity of the war without rhetoric.
stylistic_characteristics: The image that comes from a painter's eye; the rough, uneven, spoken line; the sudden visionary or biblical image inside a trench poem; the unrhymed lyric; the exact weight and colour of the physical world; the deliberate awkwardness that refuses polish.
intellectual_concerns: The war and the dead body; the Jewish East End and the immigrant poor; the painter's vision and the biblical image; death, the grave and the unquiet spirit; comradeship and the ordinary soldier; the beauty of the visible world.
historical_significance: Rosenberg is the greatest soldier-poet after Owen and the first major English poet of the Jewish immigrant working class: 'Break of Day in the Trenches' and 'Dead Man's Dump' are permanent war poems, and his visionary fragments stand with the best poetry of the period. His work is the period's clearest evidence that the war's literature came from the ranks as much as from the officers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war memoir, the historical novel and the mythographic essay
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and mythographer; the author of Good-bye to All That, I, Claudius and The White Goddess, and the most productive English man of letters of the century.
biography: Born Robert von Ranke Graves in Wimbledon on 24 July 1895, of Irish and German descent; he went from Charterhouse to the Royal Welch Fusiliers in 1914, was so badly wounded at the Somme in 1916 that he was reported dead, and published Over the Brazier (1916) and Fairies and Fusiliers (1917). He read at Oxford after the war, lived with Laura Riding in Majorca from 1929, wrote Good-bye to All That (1929), I, Claudius (1934), Claudius the God (1934) and The White Goddess (1948), held the chair of poetry at Oxford (1961–66) and died at Deià, Majorca, on 7 December 1985.
literary_profile: Graves is the period's most versatile writer: Good-bye to All That is one of the great memoirs of the war, I, Claudius and Claudius the God are the finest English historical novels of the century and became a landmark of television, and The White Goddess is one of the period's most influential — and most disputed — works of mythography. As a poet he wrote the best English love lyric of the period and kept a formal, lucid, unfashionable style through every modernist vogue.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, lucid, formal lyric in the eighteenth-century manner; the prose of the professional storyteller — swift, exact, unadorned; the first-person historical narration (Claudius); the argumentative, provocative essay of mythological speculation; the epigram and the satire.
intellectual_concerns: War and the waste of a generation; love, the beloved and the muse; the classical world and the Roman Empire; myth, the goddess and the poetic imagination; England and the English tradition; literary quarrels and the war between poet and critic.
historical_significance: Graves wrote one of the great war memoirs, the two finest English historical novels of the century, and one of the period's most influential books of mythography: Good-bye to All That changed the writing of autobiography, I, Claudius made imperial Rome a modern subject, and The White Goddess gave the period its idea of the poetic muse. He is the period's most productive and least categorisable writer.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war memoir of the English countryside and the pastoral elegy
literary_identity: Poet, critic and memoirist; the author of Undertones of War, the most lyrical prose memoir of the First World War, and a great scholar of the English rural tradition.
biography: Born Edmund Charles Blunden at Yalding, Kent, on 1 November 1896, the son of a schoolmaster; he went from Christ's Hospital to Queen's College, Oxford, but enlisted in 1915 and served on the Somme and at Ypres, winning the Military Cross. After the war he worked as a literary journalist in London and Tokyo, edited Leigh Hunt and John Clare, taught at Oxford (1931–43) and in Hong Kong (1953–64), and was professor of poetry at Oxford (1966–68). He died at Long Melford, Suffolk, on 20 January 1974.
literary_profile: Blunden wrote the most beautiful prose memoir of the war: Undertones of War (1928) records the Western Front through the eyes of a country poet, without protest and without rhetoric, and it stands with Blunden's own poems as the finest pastoral writing about the war. His scholarship on Clare, Hunt and the rural poets made him the period's great custodian of the English countryside tradition, and his poems are the best English rural verse between Thomas and Larkin.
stylistic_characteristics: The pastoral lyric in traditional measure; the exact naming of plants, streams and villages; the prose that moves as a walk moves, with a poet's eye for weather; the elegy that consoles by remembering; the understatement that refuses protest.
intellectual_concerns: The English countryside and the Kentish and Suffolk landscape; the war remembered as an intrusion on the rural world; the passing of the agricultural labourer's England; cricket, the village and the seasons; friendship and the dead of the war.
historical_significance: Blunden wrote the finest lyrical memoir of the First World War and was the period's great poet-scholar of the English countryside: Undertones of War is the pastoral counterpart to Good-bye to All That, his edition of Clare recovered a major poet, and his own verse is the best English rural poetry between Edward Thomas and Philip Larkin.
